transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date/Time: 2026-07-25 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood PM), Alex Rivera (OrionHealth CTO), Sofia Patel (OrionHealth Head of ML), James O'Neil (Platform Eng), Nina Gomez (Security)

Auto-generated Summary: Redwood walked through the Model Catalog UI and API, showing how to pick open models, compare benchmarks, and use the compatibility matrix to determine which model variants to test in a POC.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:04] Alex Rivera: yep loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:08] Luis Martinez: hi all, i'm luis, i'll take you through the catalog and the benchmark pages today and then we can jump to ops and security.
[00:12] Sofia Patel: excited, we had some questions around latency budgets and accuracy tradeoffs especially for triage workflows.
[00:20] Maya Chen: totally, we'll cover that. quick agenda: model selection, benchmark interpretation, compatibility matrix, then ops/security and next steps.
[00:30] Priya Kapoor: small note, i'll be capturing action items.

[02:05] Luis Martinez: okay starting the demo — this is the model catalog, you can filter by task, license, and our verified performance profiles. for open models we show quantized variants too, so e.g. we have llama-2 and also 8-bit and 4-bit variants in the catalog.
[02:33] James O'Neil: when you say "verified performance" what is that exactly? is it our numbers or public benchmarks?
[02:38] Luis Martinez: it's our in-house benchmarks run on standard hardware, we publish latency p50/p95, throughput at different batch sizes, and a quality score based on our eval set. sometimes there are small transcription mismatches in the model name, like —
[02:50] Sofia Patel: hah, yeah got it, good.

[04:10] Luis Martinez: here's the compatibility matrix — rows are models and columns are runtime features: kv cache, prefix caching, tensor parallelism, available quant profiles, and supported hardware (A100, H100, 4090, etc). so you can quickly see which model has a stable 4-bit path or whether it needs special kernels.
[04:35] Alex Rivera: do you have matrix entries for the custom compilation flags we run on-prem? we use some tuned kernels and a very specific sequence length distribution.
[04:44] Luis Martinez: we surface the recommended kernel families and note caveats; for very custom kernels we recommend a quick on-prem validation run. the matrix also links to the exact commit/runner we used to generate the numbers.

[06:05] Maya Chen: question for Orion: what's your expected p95 latency target for triage flows and what's acceptable throughput?
[06:15] Sofia Patel: ideally p95 < 400ms for single-turn triage, throughput around 200 qps during peak windows, but many requests are short so batching might help.
[06:28] James O'Neil: and we have a compliance requirement — all PHI must not leave our VPC, so private deployment or dedicated with strict networking.

[08:00] Luis Martinez: good, in that case we'd look at dedicated or private. For the catalog performance numbers, note the hardware column and the quant profile recommend: e.g., a 13B model in 4-bit on A100 gives roughly 120ms p50 and ~380ms p95 at batch size 1 when using our optimized kernels, while on a 4090 you might see slightly higher p95. numbers are approximate, we should run a POC to confirm.
[08:25] Sofia Patel: can you explain how KV cache impacts latency for our chat flows?
[08:31] Luis Martinez: yes — KV cache stores past keys/values so you don't recompute encoder states. for high-turn dialogues it reduces token compute but adds memory traffic; in the matrix we flag models that have incremental KV cache support. sometimes the transcript generator writes "KV cash" which is funny but —
[08:45] Alex Rivera: lol.

[10:10] Luis Martinez: on the benchmark page we have a breakdown: token-level latency, kernel occupancy, and cost per 1k tokens estimate. there's also a 'compare' view where you can overlay models and see tradeoffs — quality vs latency vs cost.
[10:32] Maya Chen: for your triage use case i'd point at two candidates: a quantized 13B and a higher-accuracy 70B 8-bit variant. 13B will be cheaper and meet latency targets most of the time; 70B gives better quality on edge cases but higher cost and more likely to hit p95.
[10:48] Sofia Patel: did you run benchmarks on our typical prompt distribution?
[10:52] Luis Martinez: not yet — that's part of the POC. if you send the prompt set and a traffic profile we'll run the same harness and publish results to your workspace.

[14:00] James O'Neil: about quantization — what's Redwood's recommended approach? dynamic vs static, and do you support GPTQ-style calibration?
[14:10] Luis Martinez: we support multiple quant flows. GPTQ/similar calibration is supported for many of the open models; we surface recommended presets in the catalog. static quant tends to be more predictable but can require calibration runs. our Optimize tooling recommends profiles based on your eval results.

[16:20] Nina Gomez: security question: do you retain logs or full request payloads in hosted mode? we need to know retention windows and encryption key control.
[16:31] Maya Chen: for hosted API we can redact or disable retention; for Dedicated and Private you can control logs and keys via your KMS/HSM. we'll share the SOC2 pack and the compliance matrix — that shows data flows and where PHI may persist.
[16:50] Nina Gomez: and SSO? we use Okta and SAML.
[16:54] Maya Chen: yes SAML/SSO and RBAC are supported in Console; we can provision roles and audit logs per team.

[19:05] Alex Rivera: pricing — can you ballpark Dedicated pricing for a baseline of 4 A100s vs hosted per-token?
[19:15] Maya Chen: ballpark only: hosted per-token for your expected volume might be cost-competitive with a small Dedicated pool, but Dedicated gives predictable throughput and network isolation. we'll send a detailed pricing and sizing spreadsheet.

[22:40] Luis Martinez: back to compatibility — some models have newer attention patterns that require updated kernels; we mark those as "experimental" in the matrix. those often need the latest runtime and sometimes H100-specific kernels for best perf.
[23:05] Sofia Patel: can we pin model versions in Redwood? we need fixed reproducibility for audits.
[23:12] Maya Chen: yes you can pin model commits and roll back; Console shows version history and per-version metrics.

[26:00] Priya Kapoor: question from sales ops, do you have a standard POC template or test harness?
[26:08] Luis Martinez: yes, we have a benchmark harness that takes a prompt set, concurrency profile, and runs across model variants and hardware; it outputs p50/p95, cost estimates, and qualitative flags. we'll share the worksheet.

[30:15] Alex Rivera: we currently use ModelHub internally and saw some regressed accuracy after quantization in a few cases. how do you measure quality regressions?
[30:25] Luis Martinez: we run unit evals and rollout tests tied to your prompt set; Optimize flags regressions and you can set alerts. the quality score in the catalog is based on the eval suite and we show diffs between model variants.

[33:40] Maya Chen: a common pattern: start with hosted for fast iteration, use dedicated for predictable peak throughput, and private when PHI cannot leave the VPC. for POC we can run a dedicated trial with network peering to your VPC so you can route traffic securely.
[34:00] Nina Gomez: network peering is interesting, do you support AWS PrivateLink or VPC peering?
[34:06] Luis Martinez: we support PrivateLink and direct connect options in Private/Dedicated deployments. specifics depend on region and account.

[37:20] Sofia Patel: what about throughput: do you recommend sharded KV caches or per-instance caching?
[37:28] Luis Martinez: typically per-instance KV cache with sharded model inference for very large models; the compatibility matrix will show recommendations per model.

[40:00] James O'Neil: can we run a benchmark that simulates our mix: 70% short single-turn triage, 30% multi-turn follow-ups?
[40:09] Luis Martinez: yep, provide the sample distribution and we can param the harness. we usually ask for a representative 500-2,000 prompt set for initial POC.

[43:50] Maya Chen: ok let's recap next steps — we'll send the model catalog deck, compatibility matrix, SOC2/security pack, and the benchmark worksheet. Orion will share the prompt set and expected traffic. Redwood SE will run the POC and publish results.
[44:10] Alex Rivera: sounds good, can we also get an example of the console view for pinned versions and metrics?
[44:18] Maya Chen: yes will include screenshots and a link to a short video.

[48:00] Luis Martinez: small note: sometimes the auto-transcription renames kernels or garbles acronyms — it may say "H one hundred" instead of H100 or mix up model names, so please treat the transcript as rough.
[48:15] Sofia Patel: understood.

[50:30] Maya Chen: last Q, timeline — we aim to start the POC next week if you can provide prompts and compliance contacts.
[50:40] Alex Rivera: we'll try to send prompts by Friday and set up a follow-up for kickoff.
[51:00] Nina Gomez: i'll coordinate the compliance questionnaire.
[51:20] Maya Chen: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up via email with the artifacts.
[51:30] Meeting End
